o: Each step simultaneously deletes every element smaller than its current left neighbor; count steps until the array is non-decreasing. Simulating deletions naively is O(n^2). Key insight: the step at which nums[i] dies equals 1 + the maximum death-step of the consecutive run of already-smaller elements immediately preceding it that it eliminates, bounded by the nearest surviving element >= nums[i] on the left.
k: Element nums[i]'s removal time = 1 + max removal time of elements it removes in one batch.
A monotonic non-increasing stack of (value, removalTime) lets us compute this in one pass.
The answer is the maximum removal time over all elements (0 if already sorted).

a.n: Approach 1: Monotonic stack with removal times
a.i: Keep a stack of surviving elements paired with the step at which they were removed (survivors have time 0 conceptually). For a new element x, pop all stack entries with value <= x; x would delete them in one step, so x's removal time is 1 + max of their times (or 0 if nothing popped, meaning x survives forever relative to the left). Push (x, t) and track the global maximum.
s: Initialize an empty stack and ans = 0.
For each x: t = 0; while stack top value <= x, t = max(t, popped time) and pop.
If the stack is non-empty after popping, t += 1 (x will be deleted by the new left neighbor).
Push (x, t); ans = max(ans, t). Return ans.
a.t: O(n) — each element is pushed and popped at most once.

w: Trace example 1 to convince yourself: 3 dies at step 1, 4 (index 2) at step 2, 6 at step 2, 8 and 5 at step 3, giving 3. Pitfall: using strict '<' instead of '<=' when popping (equal neighbors are not deleted), and forgetting that elements with no larger left neighbor never die. Follow-up: return the array after k steps, or handle deletions from both sides.
